On Sudoku-Extreme, the paper reports **99.9% accuracy** using **345× less inference compute** than the next-best model. The Hacker News title says 385×, but a commenter notes the page reports 345×.

cards.title: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest

depth.text: a study linked **stimulant products** to more **heart-problem reports**, but couldn't prove they caused the problems

The team reviewed 28,345 possible adverse-event reports in an FDA database; 854 involved energy drinks or dietary supplements containing caffeine or other stimulants. Reports involving caffeine and stimulant products were **approximately 11 times more likely to mention cardiac arrest** than reports for products without those ingredients; heart attacks appeared **about 4.5 times more frequently** in reports associated with energy drinks and stimulant supplements. Because the reports were voluntary, the study **can't establish that the products caused the events**.

cards.title: Java4Shell: pre-auth RCE flaw in Java 17 puts servers at risk (CVE-2026-114938)

depth.text: a **Java security flaw** can let attackers **run code** on some servers, sometimes without logging in

The bug is a **memory corruption** flaw in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder. Exposure requires an affected Java build, an x86-64 CPU with **AVX-512 VBMI**, and attacker-controlled data reaching the decoder. As of November 18, the post reported **no confirmed reports** of exploitation in the wild.

cards.title: Do Repeat Yourself

depth.text: someone says teams should **keep their tools** and **repeat some work** instead of forcing one stack

In the bank example, the platform team picks Go, React, and Kubernetes for everyone, and a requested chart feature gets **deprioritised**. The proposed **service-oriented architecture** instead standardizes **RESTful APIs** and their documentation, while leaving API implementation to each team.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say copying is cheaper than a bad shared abstraction; others want shared UI standards and gradual migration to avoid a disjointed product.

comments.text: Sometimes syntactic duplication can give you a hint to underlying semantic duplication. But it's no more than a hint. DRY doesn't mean don't repeat a similar looking block of code, it means try to structure your code so that each element of the design has a single representation. There's no shortcut to good design where no thinking is required, much as a lot of people seem to wish there were.
Or as the go proverb goes "a little copying is better than a little dependency" ( https://go-proverbs.github.io/ )

After a couple years of integrating through shared APIs, new management is trying to force us all into a single platform - Go and Node+React. We have thousands of years of combined experience in our various technologies and we are…

The first thing you have to do is disable a bunch of logging that no one uses, as that can cripple the performance of your app. Then you have to go update a bunch of dependencies with security problems. Then you have to fix their git hooks. Which is to say, standard does not imply good. A lot of times companies just standardize…

glossary.FTSE 250: A UK stock-market index made up of 250 companies; the article uses it to describe the company being audited.
glossary.decision model: A program that weighs possible choices and predicts or selects one.
glossary.PII: Personally Identifiable Information: details that could identify someone, such as an email or phone number.
glossary.threshold: The score a system must reach before it takes an action.
glossary.false positive: A system reports a match even though the person is not the one it was looking for.
glossary.false negative: When a check misses a problem that is really there.
glossary.regex: A pattern used to find or check text.
glossary.embeddings: Numbers that represent the meaning of text so software can search or compare it.
glossary.model router: A tool that picks which AI model handles a task.
glossary.calibrated model: A model whose confidence scores match how often its answers are right.
glossary.benchmarks: Tests people use to compare how well different models perform.
glossary.inference speed: How quickly a model produces answers when you use it.
glossary.multimodal: Able to work with more than one kind of input, such as text and images.
glossary.amino acid: One of the small building blocks that proteins are made from.
glossary.protein language model: An AI trained on protein sequences to learn their patterns and make predictions about them.
glossary.shuffled control: A test version with the same letters rearranged, used to check whether a model depends on their order.
glossary.residue: One amino acid building block in a protein.
glossary.RCE: Remote Code Execution: a flaw that lets an attacker make a computer run their commands from somewhere else.
glossary.memory corruption: When a program accidentally changes stored information it was not supposed to touch.
glossary.Base64: A way to represent data as ordinary text characters, even when the data itself is not text.
glossary.x86-64: A kind of computer code understood by many PC processors.
glossary.AVX-512 VBMI: Special processor instructions that let some computers handle many bytes at once.
glossary.OpenJDK: The open-source project that develops Java.
glossary.audit: A check of whether an organization’s financial records are complete and match what it did.
glossary.standalone reporting entity: A separate part of an organization whose finances are reported on and checked separately.
glossary.assets: Things an organization owns or controls that have value.
glossary.liabilities: Money an organization owes or bills it needs to pay.
glossary.CFO: Chief Financial Officer: the person responsible for overseeing an organization’s finances.
glossary.heap: Memory a program can request as it runs, useful when it doesn’t know in advance how much space its data will need.
glossary.CVSS: Common Vulnerability Scoring System: a scale people use to rate how serious a security flaw is.
glossary.rightsholder: A person or organization that owns rights to something, such as copyrighted material.
glossary.ISP: Internet Service Provider: a company that connects people to the internet.
glossary.splinternet: A split-up Internet where countries or regions have different rules or access.
glossary.exploitation: Using a software flaw to make a computer do something its makers did not intend.
glossary.reverse engineering: Figuring out how a program works by examining the program itself.
glossary.CTF: Capture the Flag: a security game where players solve challenges to find a hidden answer.
glossary.zero-day: A security flaw attackers can use before its maker has a fix.
glossary.arbitration: A way to settle a dispute with a neutral decision-maker instead of a judge or jury.
glossary.SSO: Single Sign-On: a way to use one sign-in for several work services.
glossary.eclipse: When one object disappears behind another or into its shadow; Io disappears into Jupiter’s shadow.
glossary.finite speed: A speed that is limited, so light takes time to get from one place to another instead of arriving instantly.
glossary.stellar aberration: Stars seem to shift slightly across the sky during the year because Earth moves while their light travels.
glossary.AI Overview: A Google-made summary placed above ordinary search results, with links to the pages it used.
glossary.SEO: Search engine optimization: making changes to a webpage so it is more likely to appear in search results.
glossary.GEO: Generative Engine Optimization: work to help content show up in answers from AI search tools.
glossary.CTR: Click-through rate: the share of people who see a result and then click it.
glossary.referring domain: A website that links to another website.
glossary.jqXHR: jQuery's object for a web request, which holds information about the request and its response.
glossary.ReDoS: Regular expression denial of service: a flaw where crafted text can make matching code take an extremely long time.
glossary.querySelectorAll: A browser method that finds all page elements matching a selector.
glossary.form-associated custom elements: Custom HTML elements that can take part in a form, such as sending a value when the form is submitted.
glossary.XML: Extensible Markup Language: a way to label pieces of information so computers can store and exchange them.
glossary.fine-grained reactivity: A way for an app to update only the parts affected when data changes, rather than refreshing everything.
glossary.reactive graph: A map of how pieces of app data depend on each other, so the app knows what needs updating when something changes.
glossary.Promise: A value that will arrive later, like the result of a request to fetch data.
glossary.async iterator: A sequence of values that arrive over time rather than all at once.
glossary.server functions: Functions called from an app that run on a server instead of on the user's device.
glossary.RPC: Remote Procedure Call: a way for one program to ask another program to do something directly.
glossary.Server Sent Events: A way for a server to keep sending updates over one open connection.
glossary.ONNX Runtime: A tool that lets software run machine-learning models.
glossary.evals: Short tests used to check how well a model handles tasks you care about.
glossary.fork: A separate copy of a shared software project that people can take in a different direction.
glossary.telemetry: Information a program sends back about how it is being used or whether it is working properly.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.OAuth tokens: Digital passes that let an app use an account without needing the account’s password.
glossary.warm leads: People who may be interested in buying because they already have a connection to the seller.
glossary.YC: Y Combinator: a group that gives young startups funding and advice.
glossary.ADL: Argument-dependent lookup: a C++ rule that helps find a function based on the kinds of values passed to it.
glossary.ArbCom: Arbitration Committee: Wikipedia's group for handling serious disputes between editors and imposing sanctions.
glossary.NPOV: Neutral point of view: Wikipedia's rule for presenting subjects without taking sides.
glossary.doxxed: Having someone's private identifying details exposed online, often to intimidate them.
glossary.read-only: You can look at the information, but you can’t change it or add anything.
glossary.pull request: A proposal to add your code changes to a shared project, usually asking others to review them first.
glossary.difference-in-differences: A way to compare how results change over time at firms that adopt a tool and firms that have not yet adopted it.
glossary.confidence interval: A range of values the researchers say their estimate could plausibly fall within.
glossary.working paper: A research paper shared while it is still being developed, rather than a finished, peer-reviewed journal article.
glossary.DOM: Document Object Model: the browser's list of the pieces that make up a webpage.
glossary.XSS: Cross-site scripting: A flaw that can make a website run instructions supplied by someone visiting it.
glossary.CSRF: Cross-site request forgery: tricking a signed-in browser into sending a request the user didn’t intend.
glossary.event loop: The browser’s turn-taking system for handling code, clicks, and other events.
glossary.rendering pipeline: The steps a browser takes to turn a page’s code into what appears on screen.
glossary.accessibility tree: A version of a webpage’s content that tools like screen readers use to explain it to people.
glossary.canvas: A webpage area where code can draw pictures or other visuals.
glossary.WebAssembly: A way to run compiled programs inside a web browser.
glossary.TLD: Top-Level Domain: the ending of a web address, like .com.
glossary.layout engine: The part of a browser that decides where text and other things go on a page.
glossary.SOA: Service-Oriented Architecture: a way to build software from separate parts that interact through agreed rules.
glossary.REST: A common way for one app to send requests to another app over a network.
glossary.DRY: Don't Repeat Yourself: a guideline to avoid writing the same code in several places.
glossary.Kubernetes: A system for running and managing software containers across computers.
